title: Transatlantic Biotech Spurs Cancer Breakthroughs
content:
The advances are astounding. A personalized cancer vaccine developed with messenger RNA (mRNA) technology extends the survival of melanoma patients. It trains patients’ immune systems to recognize and attack unique mutated proteins found only on their tumor cells. Another new mRNA drug, Daraxonrasib, doubles the life expectancy of pancreatic cancer patients.

These breakthroughs result from longstanding cooperation between US and European researchers and firms.

Start with the basic research. In 2005, Hungarian Katalin Karikó and American Drew Weissman at the University of Pennsylvania showed that modifying the nucleoside building blocks of synthetic mRNA could reduce unwanted inflammatory responses while improving protein production. Their work helped make therapeutic mRNA viable and later earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize.

The technology then moved across the Atlantic.

Germany’s BioNTech pursued mRNA and individualized cancer immunotherapies long before the COVID-19 pandemic. When the pandemic arrived, BioNTech partnered with US pharma giant Pfizer to develop and distribute the COVID vaccine.

title: Russia Attacks – Would NATO Freeze?
content:
Would NATO fight if Russia entered its territory? Yes, says CEPA Fellow Skip Davis, but it’s also the case that alliance readiness has been increased across the eastern flank in the last decade and now extends far beyond the ability to meet an armed attack.

Question: What would happen on the ground if Russian troops crossed into NATO territory? Would alliance commanders need to await permission to engage?

Davis: NATO forward land forces are multinational battle groups and brigades stationed on the eastern flank, mostly in countries bordering Russia. They have a lead nation, but they’re established in nine different countries along the east, from Finland all the way down to Romania, all the Baltics, Poland and Slovakia, Hungary. Under NATO doctrine, they have the right to respond in self-defense. They would not need permission to respond.

But that is the simplest response. We have to peel the onion a little bit because Russia would normally be expected to do some type of preparation.

title: The Czechs: 1938 and All That
content:
October 28 is the 108th anniversary of the creation of the Czechoslovak Republic, a new but old country wrenched from the talons of the dying Austro-Hungarian Empire in 1918.

September 30, meanwhile, marked the 88th anniversary of the Munich Agreement, when the country was abandoned by its allies, and its German-speaking borderlands sliced off and handed to Herr Hitler.

It’s always a time for soul-searching. Politicians, historians and the media ponder what went wrong in the 20 years after 1918, and what’s gone right in the 37 years since 1989.

These days, with a new war raging to the country’s east, the soul-searching can get fraught, and at times hysterical.

“We’re living in 1938. It’s just a question of which month,” is a typical response from doom-mongers on X scouring the horizon for signs of Russian tank divisions rolling past the Tesco’s in Prague 10.

“Never mind 1938. It’s already 1939,” say others, peering anxiously at the skies for drones.

It’s not.

Czechoslovakia’s fate was awful, but it’s hard to see any other outcome given the set of circumstances in which Central Europe’s sole surviving democracy found itself in 1938.

title: Putin and His War Without End
content:
One characteristic of dictators and despots is that they speak for as long as they like. It’s a defining feature that brevity is discarded while verbosity prospers. Putin offered a good example when he used an address at the Valdai Forum on October 1 to ramble on for 3 hours and 20 minutes. There then followed a moderated discussion on stage.

For those seeking a clue about the Kremlin’s future direction of Kremlin, there were some hints. The bad news is that these were mostly extremely bleak.

Five key points of his strategy can be gleaned from his lengthy remarks:

1. Offense is defense

Putin’s central strategy and his ultimate goal is to reframe every instance of Russian aggression as a defensive necessity. He claims that Russia is merely responding to Western attacks or provocations.

This narrative is the foundation of his entire policy:

Putin justifies the war of aggression against Ukraine as a defense against the aggressive West. It is fair to summarize his statements as showing that he is preparing the population for a protracted confrontation while portraying every escalation — past and future — as a “response” and never as a Russian initiative.

title: The US Bets Big on Eurasia
content:
It seemed likely when Donald Trump took office that the South Caucasus and Central Asia would not receive much attention. US administrations have long had an on-off interest, and there was little obvious sign of change.

How wrong that was. Events on the sidelines of the 2026 United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) showed a new and vigorous focus, including significant high-level engagement.

There was intensified focus on the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) and Trans-Caspian connectivity. Bringing senior US officials and private investors together with leaders from the South Caucasus and Central Asia, the discussions made clear that Washington is moving its Trans-Caspian agenda from geopolitical concept toward commercial reality.

title: A Time to Reap: Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi
content:
Ukraine is entering winter with another demonstration of military brilliance, an exhausted population that still refuses to surrender, and Western partners who continue to mistake caution for strategy — effectively inviting Russia to test lines that have not been red for a long time and yet are crimson with blood.

Operation Vivaldi in northern Donetsk Oblast has been a triumph. The 3rd Army Corps has combined electronic warfare, air defense, aerial drones, and unmanned ground vehicles in an offensive around Lyman. Ukrainian forces say they have restored control over 125 sq km (48 sq miles), a significant advance in a war of attrition.

Ukraine even successfully reintroduced tanks, armored vehicles, and elements of mechanized maneuver into a battlefield increasingly dominated by drones and positional warfare.

title: Russia: A Menu of Death in Ukraine’s Small Towns
content:
Russia’s attacks on civilians and refusal of humanitarian aid for besieged frontline Ukrainians in the occupied territories have become a powerful symbol of the Kremlin’s barbarism. In recent weeks, the results of this anti-humanitarian campaign have been highlighted in the small, occupied town of Oleshky.

Conditions are critical in the town, which sits on a tributary river southeast of Kherson, the town liberated by Ukraine in 2023. Occupied since 2022, when it had a population of 24,000, its remaining residents are trapped without food, electricity, or proper medical help. They are pinned in their homes by the constant threat of Russian drones, mines, and artillery. Water is scarce; there have been no supplies for four months, and some are said to be eating dogs to survive.

Oleshky has made headlines and inspired campaigns around the world, but it is far from unique in the war-ravaged Kherson region. People in other settlements also face the choice of starving to death or taking their chances under fire.

title: AI: Let’s Not Pause Progress
content:
AI bots hide mistakes. They make up data and move files without permission. In response, some call for a ban on superintelligence, while others demand a pause or slowdown. 

Either move would be a mistake. Despite genuine fears about safety, an AI slowdown will prove unworkable. 

Consider the challenge of global action. Even if one views a ban, pause, or slowdown as desirable, ask yourself what China will do? Beijing called Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s “We must pace the frontier” warning “fearmongering,” suggesting that the alarm about AI was a US plot to hinder China’s own innovation.  If China isn’t on board, capable AI models will be available regardless of what the US does.

The recent summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump underlined this impasse. No deal to slow or pause AI progress emerged. Instead, Trump said the two leaders “didn’t spend that much time talking about it” and that he had little interest in working with China on AI because “we’re leading by a lot.”

title: Russia’s Rage Fixes on the British
content:
British statecraft has “lived free in Russia’s head” for hundreds of years, in the words of a former UK defense attaché in Moscow. The historian Mark Galeotti noted that, over the last century, “Perfidious Albion” was, in Russia’s eyes, its “most cunning and devious foe”.

From this soil, fed by £25 bn ($33 bn) of UK aid to Ukraine since 2022, has emerged an eruption of suspicion and hostility. It may yet produce something more menacing than the current torrent of Kremlin-inspired verbal barrages.

Russia is run in part by a siloviki of former Soviet security officials who were spoon-fed distrust of the British as part of their training. It is part of their lore that London did terrible harm to the Bolsheviks and then the Soviet era, and that British intelligence chalked up significant triumphs at their expense. In this worldview, British attempts to undermine Russian power and greatness are part of an old game.

The flip side is the strange magnetism of Britain for the Russian elite; there have been massive Russian investments in British real estate, academia, and legal and financial sectors which have led to the sobriquet ‘Londongrad’ for the second home of many oligarchs.

title: FSB Focuses Crosshairs on Russian Exiles
content:
While European governments confront the escalation of Russian sabotage activities, the FSB has stepped up its efforts on another, less-observed front – the targeting of Russian exiles. Less than two weeks after the US revealed a Russian plot to assassinate dissidents in Washington, the FSB turned its crosshairs on London.

On September 28, the FSB announced the launch of a criminal investigation on terrorism charges against Ksenia Maximova, leader of the Russian Democratic Society UK. At the end of the communique, the service added an ominous line: “Russia’s FSB will continue its efforts to neutralize terrorist activities instigated by London using Russian expatriates.”
